tip: In Dutch you congratulate someone met (with) a thing, not on it: gefeliciteerd met je verjaardag.
Weather verbs use a placeholder subject het: het regent means it rains, with no real thing doing it.
Dutch names the posture of a located thing: upright items staan, so de soep staat op tafel, not just is.
Adjectives add -e before a noun: schoon becomes schone in een schone kamer.
Drop the -e when a neuter (het) noun follows een: een lief kind, not een lieve kind, since it is het kind.
Opbellen splits in a main clause: the op prefix jumps to the end, belde haar ouders ... op.
Dutch uses lopen for the course of a path or road: het fietspad loopt, literally the bike path walks.
Adjectives double as adverbs with no extra ending: stil covers both quiet and quietly, as in viel stil.
Comparisons use the ending -er plus dan for than: comfortabeler dan het harde.
Around wraps the noun in om ... heen, one word each side: om het meer heen means around the lake.
Say by a vehicle with met, not a word for by: met de auto means by car.
Kijken pairs with naar to mean watch: keek naar het journaal is watched the news.
Direction down something goes after it with af: de trap af means down the stairs.
Our is ons before a neuter (het) noun and onze elsewhere: ons huis, because it is het huis.
For the best within a group, Dutch marks the group with van, not in: het modernste museum van de stad.
Start with an als clause and the main verb comes right after the comma: Als je wilt, kun je.
The Dutch half points to the next hour: half acht means 7:30, half toward eight, not 8:30.
Units of measure stay singular after a number: twee uur for two hours, never twee uren.
Of means whether in an indirect yes-no question: weet niet of haar broer komt, doesn't know whether he comes.
Dutch has no verb for liking to do something; add graag to the verb: danst graag means likes to dance.
Er works as there in there-are statements: er staan zeventig containers means there are seventy containers.
In a passive the doer follows door for by: is geblokkeerd door een ongeluk means is blocked by an accident.
Dutch turns transport nouns into verbs: from fiets comes fietsen, so hij fietst means he cycles.
A goal to plus a verb becomes om ... te: om eerst te sparen means to save first.
A comparative before a noun still adds -e: duur becomes duurdere in de duurdere wijn.
Helpen takes met for help with: hielp haar moeder met het huishouden, helped with the housework.
Tot marks until up to a time or point: tot sluitingstijd means until closing time.
Elkaar is the reciprocal each other, one word for a two-way action: elkaar voorstellen, introduce each other.
